input.body:
Shepherd publishes the fleet dashboard, and today every viewer of it reads GitHub anonymously at 60 requests/hour per IP — which one fleet sweep exceeds — or pastes a token. The Sign in button is built and waiting on two things only an account owner can create.

The mechanics that used to be manual are not any more: `claudinite-dashboard` now ships a `deploy-oauth-exchange` task ([missingbulb/Claudinite#942](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/942)) that uploads the endpoint, routes it and verifies the URL answers. What is left here is the registration, two secrets and a variable, and one config edit.

## Steps

- [ ] **Register a GitHub App** on the `missingbulb` account, with *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled.
  - Read-only **Contents**, **Issues**, **Metadata**, **Actions**.
  - Callback URL: `https://missingbulb.github.io/` with **wildcard matching**, which covers every project Pages site on that host.
  - Note the **Client ID**; generate a **Client secret**.
  - *While absent:* no Sign in button renders; the token box is the only way in.

- [ ] **Install the App** on the `missingbulb` account, so a user token can see the member repos.
  - *While absent:* sign-in succeeds but every member row reads as not visible to you — the token carries no installation.

- [ ] **Set `clientId`** on this repo's `claudinite-dashboard` declaration `config`. It is public — it appears in every authorize URL — so it belongs in the declaration and not in a secret. The deploy refuses to run without it, because the endpoint is minted for one app.

- [ ] **Set two repo Actions secrets** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Secrets).
  - `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — scoped to **Account · Workers Scripts · Edit** and nothing else.
  - `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` — the App's client secret.
  - *While either is absent:* the run parks the item at `task:status:needs-human-action` naming the missing one; nothing else breaks.

- [ ] **Set one repo variable** (same page, **Variables** tab): `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`. Not a secret — it is in every Cloudflare dashboard URL its owner opens — and since [missingbulb/Claudinite#1494](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1494) the executor hands every repository variable to code-work with nothing declared.
  - *While absent:* the run fails naming it, since nothing declares it and the queue therefore cannot park on it.

- [ ] **Run the task**: `create-work-item claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange`. It reports the deployed URL and whether it is wired. `allowedOrigins` needs no setting — it defaults to `https://missingbulb.github.io`, which is this deployment's origin.

- [ ] **Set `exchangeUrl`** to the URL that run reported, on the same declaration entry. This is the last step and the one that makes the button appear: `clientId` alone does nothing.

## Closing condition

Loading the deployed dashboard signed out shows **Sign in with GitHub**; clicking it returns you signed in, with the rate pill reading `…/5000 · user` and a member repo rendering — and no token ever typed.

---

Answering your question first, because the premise is off in a way that changes the cost.

**`claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml` is not bespoke, and it's not only the deploy.** It's a canon stub at [`packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml), seeded into each declaring member's `.github/workflows/` at adoption via the pack's `seedOps`. It does three things: decides whether to build at all (a cache key over the mount and settings — the scheduler finishes hourly and almost always nothing moved), runs `build-site.mjs` **out of the mount**, then deploys to Pages. So the build logic converges with the canon; only the workflow is frozen.

I checked whether I was wrong about "frozen": `converge-workflows.mjs` is misleadingly named — its own header says *"SCAFFOLDED, NEVER CONVERGED"*, same reason as always. So editing the stub reaches new adopters at once and existing members only through a human-merged PR into their `.github/`, which is the cost you've offered to absorb.

So yes — I can do it, and it's cheap here since realistically Shepherd is the deployment. Two notes on how I'd do it: named lines (`CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.… }}`), not the `toJSON(vars)` bag, because this workflow isn't a function of any task set so #1296's wedge doesn't apply, and named lines spare the dashboard pack from duplicating a bag parser it can't import across packs. And I'd have to fold the values into the cache key, or changing the variable wouldn't republish the site.

**`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is done** and pushed to [PR #1465](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1465) — it needed no workflow edit at all, since #1494 already hands every repo variable to code-work. `required_secrets` is now the two real credentials; the worker names the variable itself when unset, because nothing declares it and the queue therefore can't park on it. Two new assertions, both watched failing first. Full suite 2824/2824, `check_the_work` clean, `check_the_world` 0 blocking. [Shepherd#352](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/352) now says variable, not secret.

The remaining piece is a decision rather than a fact, so:

Both values are public and belong in a reviewable diff, and the pack's other eight config keys (mode, owner, exclude, canonRepo, redirectUri…) already live there — moving two of them splits one config surface across two stores. Changing them republishes the site automatically, because the cache key hashes the settings file.

Costs a human-merged PR into each existing dashboard member's .github/, and the pack's config then lives in two places.

content.text: Now the workflow stub — the two named vars, and folding them into the cache key so a change still republishes:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml'
s=open(p).read()

old = """      - name: What the page would be built from
        id: sources
        run: echo "key=dashboard-deployed-${{ hashFiles('.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/**', '.claudinite/shared/engine/**', '.claudinite-settings.json', '.claudinite-checks.json', '**/*.GENERATED.json') }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT\""""
new = """      - name: What the page would be built from
        id: sources
        env:
          # Through `env:` rather than inline in `run:`: a repository variable is text
          # an owner typed into a settings box, and interpolating it straight into a
          # shell line makes that box a command.
          CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID }}
          CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL }}
        run: |
          # The sign-in pair are repository variables, so no file hash covers them.
          # Without this a change to either would hit the cache, skip the build, and
          # leave the site serving the previous client id indefinitely — the silent
          # half of "is that already deployed?". Hashed rather than embedded so a
          # value's own characters cannot break the key.
          signin=$(printf '%s|%s' "$CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID" "$CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL" | sha256sum | cut -c1-16)
          echo "key=dashboard-deployed-${{ hashFiles('.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/**', '.claudinite/shared/engine/**', '.claudinite-settings.json', '.claudinite-checks.json', '**/*.GENERATED.json') }}-$signin" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT\""""
assert old in s

Sign-in's client id and exchange URL are repository variables

They are the two values an owner sets while standing in the GitHub App's
settings, and the exchange URL is minted by a deploy rather than authored — so
requiring a commit to record it put a merge between the endpoint going live and
the button appearing. Neither is a secret: the client id is in every authorize
URL and the exchange URL is fetched by the browser.

That key exists to skip the build when nothing moved, and no file hash covers a
repository variable — without this, changing either would hit the cache and
leave the site serving the previous client id with nothing to show for it.

One reader, `deployment-config.mjs`, resolves them for both the site build and
the deploy task, so the endpoint cannot be minted for a different App than the
button authorizes against. A declaration still carrying `clientId`/`exchangeUrl`
is read as the fallback and reported once: nothing converges a member's own
settings file, so a deployment configured before this must keep its button.

input.body:
Shepherd publishes the fleet dashboard, and today every viewer of it reads GitHub anonymously at 60 requests/hour per IP — which one fleet sweep exceeds — or pastes a token. The Sign in button is built and waiting on two things only an account owner can create.

The mechanics that used to be manual are not any more: `claudinite-dashboard` now ships a `deploy-oauth-exchange` task ([missingbulb/Claudinite#942](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/942)) that uploads the endpoint, routes it and verifies the URL answers. What is left here is the registration, two secrets, three variables, and one re-seeded workflow.

Everything below except the App registration lives in **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**.

## Steps

- [ ] **Register a GitHub App** on the `missingbulb` account, with *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled.
  - Read-only **Contents**, **Issues**, **Metadata**, **Actions**.
  - Callback URL: `https://missingbulb.github.io/` with **wildcard matching**, which covers every project Pages site on that host.
  - Note the **Client ID**; generate a **Client secret**.
  - *While absent:* no Sign in button renders; the token box is the only way in.

- [ ] **Install the App** on the `missingbulb` account, so a user token can see the member repos.
  - *While absent:* sign-in succeeds but every member row reads as not visible to you — the token carries no installation.

- [ ] **Re-seed `.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml`** from the pack's current stub. It gains two `vars` lines and a cache-key change. `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so this is a PR someone merges — once.
  - *While absent:* the sign-in variables below never reach the build, and the site keeps publishing without a button however they are set.

- [ ] **Set two secrets** (Secrets tab).
  - `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — scoped to **Account · Workers Scripts · Edit** and nothing else.
  - `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` — the App's client secret.
  - *While either is absent:* the deploy run parks the item at `task:status:needs-human-action` naming the missing one; nothing else breaks.

- [ ] **Set two variables** (Variables tab).
  - `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` — the account hosting the endpoint. Not a secret: it is in every Cloudflare dashboard URL its owner opens.
  - `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID` — the App's client id. Not a secret either: it appears in every authorize URL the page builds.
  - *While the account id is absent:* the deploy fails naming it — nothing declares it, so the queue cannot park on it.

- [ ] **Run the task**: `create-work-item claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange`. It reports the deployed URL and whether it is wired. `allowedOrigins` needs no setting — it defaults to `https://missingbulb.github.io`, which is this deployment's origin.

- [ ] **Set `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL`** to the URL that run reported. This is the last step and the one that makes the button appear: the client id alone does nothing. Changing it republishes the site, because the deploy workflow folds both variables into its cache key.

## Closing condition

Loading the deployed dashboard signed out shows **Sign in with GitHub**; clicking it returns you signed in, with the rate pill reading `…/5000 · user` and a member repo rendering — and no token ever typed.

```
Folders touched (this round)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
packs/claudinite-dashboard/
  declared-config.mjs → deployment-config.mjs, now owning WHICH STORE
  each key lives in: the sign-in pair resolve from repository variables,
  falling back to a declaration that still carries them and naming every
  key that fell back. build-site.mjs prints that note; pack.mjs drops

packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/
  The Pages stub passes both vars (through env:, not inline in run:) and

packs/claudinite-dashboard/tasks/deploy-oauth-exchange/
  Reads the client id through the same resolver the page uses; the
  account id is a variable, not a declared secret; the wiring note names
```

Three things worth flagging:

**The cache key was the real trap.** That workflow skips the build when a hash over the mount and settings is unchanged — and no file hash covers a repo variable. Without folding them in, changing either would hit the cache, skip the build, and leave the site serving the previous client id with nothing anywhere to show for it. It's hashed into the key rather than embedded so a value's own characters can't break it.

**I kept the declaration as a fallback**, with a `NOTE:` line on every build that uses it. Nothing converges a member's settings file, so a deployment that had configured `clientId`/`exchangeUrl` would otherwise lose its button on the next build. It's the migration, not a second supported store — the README row is marked legacy.

**One test was passing vacuously and I fixed it.** My first cache-key assertion checked the whole workflow step, which still contains `sha256sum` and both variable names in its own `env:` — so it stayed green with the digest dropped from the key, the exact bug it exists for. It now asserts on the key line itself, and fails under that mutation. Two of my three planned mutations bit first time; this one didn't, which is why I ran them.

That's the human-merged PR you offered to approve — once, and only for repos already running the dashboard.

> ⚠️ Still open: [PR #1465](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1465) awaiting your review. [Shepherd#352](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/352) now needs the App registered, two secrets, two variables, the Pages stub re-seeded, then the task run and `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` set.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

mkdir -p packs/basics/skills/writing-handover-issues && cat > packs/basics/skills/writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: writing-handover-issues
description: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
---

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Where a step's output is a value the reader must hold, that is a reason to keep the list
short and linear, not to add a note reminding them.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.
EOF

input.body:
Give the fleet dashboard a Sign in button. Nine steps, one sitting; everything below the checklist is background.

- [ ] Register a GitHub App named `Claudinite Dashboard` — [new App](https://github.com/settings/apps/new)
- [ ] Set its **Homepage URL** and **Callback URL** to `https://missingbulb.github.io/`, and tick **Enable Device Flow**'s neighbour *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation*
- [ ] Under **Permissions → Repository**, set Contents, Issues, Metadata and Actions to **Read-only**, then press **Create GitHub App**
- [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — on the App's General page, under the app name; begins `Iv23`
- [ ] Press **Generate a new client secret** on that same page, and copy the value shown under **Client secrets** — it is displayed once
- [ ] Install the App on `missingbulb` — the **Install App** tab in the left sidebar of that page
- [ ] Copy your Cloudflare **Account ID** — [Workers overview](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/workers), right-hand sidebar under *Account details*; a 32-character hex string
- [ ] Create a Cloudflare API token with the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** template — [new token](https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens), then **Create Token**; copy the value shown once on the confirmation screen
- [ ] Add secret `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` (the client secret) — [new secret](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/settings/secrets/actions/new)
- [ ] Add secret `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` (the API token) — [new secret](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/settings/secrets/actions/new)
- [ ] Add variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` (the Account ID) — [new variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/settings/variables/actions/new)
- [ ] Add variable `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID` (the Client ID) — [new variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/settings/variables/actions/new)
- [ ] Merge the PR that re-seeds `.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml` from the pack's current stub
- [ ] Run the deploy: `create-work-item claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange`, and copy the `https://…workers.dev` URL it reports
- [ ] Add variable `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` (that URL) — [new variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/settings/variables/actions/new)

**Done when** loading the [dashboard](https://missingbulb.github.io/Shepherd/) in a signed-out window shows **Sign in with GitHub**, and clicking it returns you signed in with the rate pill reading `…/5000 · user`.

---

## Background

**Why.** Every viewer of the dashboard today reads GitHub anonymously at 60 requests/hour per IP — which one fleet sweep exceeds — or pastes a token. A static page cannot reuse your github.com login, so a Sign in button is the only alternative, and it needs an App plus a hosted `code` → token exchange.

**What each part buys, and what stays broken until it is done:**

| Undone | Effect |
|---|---|
| The App is not registered | No Sign in button renders anywhere; the token box is the only way in |
| The App is not installed on `missingbulb` | Sign-in succeeds, but every member row reads *not visible to you* — the token carries no installation |
| Either secret is missing | The deploy run parks at `task:status:needs-human-action` naming it; nothing else breaks |
| `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is missing | The deploy fails naming it — nothing declares it, so the queue cannot park on it |
| The workflow is not re-seeded | The sign-in variables never reach the site build, so the button never appears however they are set |
| `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` is unset | The page renders the token box; the client id alone does nothing |

**Why some of these are variables and not secrets.** Neither the client id nor the exchange URL is confidential — the first is in every authorize URL the page builds, the second is fetched by the browser. The Cloudflare account id is in every dashboard URL you open. Secrets are only the two real credentials.

**Why the workflow needs a merge.** `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write. The new stub passes the two sign-in variables to the build and folds them into its deploy cache key — without that, changing either would hit the cache and leave the site serving the previous client id.

**Why the API token is that narrow.** The *Edit Cloudflare Workers* template grants Workers Scripts · Edit and nothing else. The deploy uploads one script and reads the account's `workers.dev` subdomain; it needs no more.

Mechanics: [missingbulb/Claudinite#942](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/942) and the task's [README](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/claudinite-dashboard/tasks/deploy-oauth-exchange/README.md).

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).

- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

attachment.snippet: 1 claudinite-dashboard 2 3 A read-only view of what a repo's — or a fleet's — Claudinite is doing: what is stuck, 4 what is queued, what has run, and what the corpus has been costing and catching. 5 6 **Two modes, and a deployment states which one it is.** `mode` is `"repo"` — that 7 repo's own page — or `"fleet"` — the overview across a roster. It is the one key with 8 **no default**: the build refuses to publish a deployment that did not say, and refuses 9 a mode that contradicts the rest of the config (`fleet` naming no roster source, 10 `repo` naming one). 11 12 It used to be inferred: a config that named where more than one member came from was a 13 fleet, and silence was a repo page. That reads fine until a fleet deployment loses its 14 roster source — a dropped key, a renamed artifact, an enumeration that was never 15 configured — and publishes a one-repo dashboard that looks entirely intentional. An 16 inference cannot tell "this repo only" from "the fleet, whose members went missing"; 17 a stated mode can, and the disagreement becomes a failed build instead of a quietly 18 wrong site. 19 20 **Opt-in.** Nothing fingerprints it and `--init` never seeds it: a repo carries this 21 because someone declared it. Adopting it wires the GitHub Pages deploy. 22 23 ## Adopting it 24 25 ```jsonc 26 // .claudinite-settings.json 27 { "packs": ["claudinite-dashboard"] } 28 ``` 29 30 That is the whole of it for a member: the dashboard covers this repo, signs in with a 31 pasted token, and publishes to Pages. Adoption seeds 32 [the deploy workflow](stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml) into 33 `.github/workflows/`, and **you must enable Pages with source *GitHub Actions*** — a 34 repository setting no Action can flip; until then the deploy job is the only thing 35 that fails. 36 37 Everything else is optional `config` on the declaration: 38 39 | Key | Default | What it buys | 40 |---|---|---| 41 | `mode` | **none — required** | `"repo"` or `"fleet"`. The build fails without it, and fails when it disagrees with the roster keys below | 42 | `owner` | — | Whose repos this deployment covers. The page **enumerates them in the browser, as the viewer** — so this is a fleet deployment, and the fleet a person sees is exactly the fleet they can read. The way to build a fleet dashboard | 43 | `exclude` | none | Repos under that owner that are not members (either `owner/name` or the bare name). Archived and forked repos leave by their own state | 44 | `repos` | — | An explicit member list instead, for a deployment that wants a fixed set | 45 | `rosterFile` | — | A generated artifact in the repo listing members — the legacy shape, still read | 46 | `canonRepo` | — | The repo whose live engine and pack versions member stamps are compared against; unset means freshness reads *unknown* rather than being guessed | 47 | `clientId`, `exchangeUrl` | — | Both together turn on **Sign in with GitHub**; either alone does nothing | 48 | `redirectUri` | the page's URL | Override when the callback differs | 49 | `defaultRepo` | this repo | Which repo a single-repo deployment shows | 50 51 ## Why a pack and not engine code 52 53 Nothing converges, scheduler runs or executes because the dashboard exists, and a member that 54 never looks at it should not carry it. Engine code is what every member *runs*; this 55 is content a member opts into. Being a pack also buys it a version and migration 56 lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment at which the deploy can be 57 wired — none of which engine code has. 58 59 It has **two views**, and which one you land on is the URL: 60 61 - **Fleet** — every member at once, worst first. What a deployment with a roster 62 opens on. 63 - **Repo** — one member's scheduler in full. Reached by clicking a member, or 64 `?repo=owner/name` directly. 65 66 A deployment with one member (or none) goes straight to the repo view: a one-row 67 fleet overview would be nothing but a click in the way. 68 69 ## Running it locally 70 71 ```sh 72 node packs/claudinite-dashboard/serve.mjs missingbulb/Claudinite 73 ``` 74 75 ## Two kinds of data, read two different ways 76 77 Everything on both pages is one of two things, and the difference is the whole reason 78 the page can afford what it shows. 79 80 **What is true right now** is a live read, and there are few of them: the repo, its 81 head commit, one page of issues, one page of Actions runs. All are ETag-revalidated, 82 and a `304` costs no rate-limit budget at all. 83 84 **What happened before** is one file: the repo's own 85 `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`, folded hourly by the 86 [usage-fold task](../claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/README.md) in the 87 claudinite-growth pack. It is content at a sha, so it is read once when the default 88 branch moves and **not at all** while it has not. input.title: A handover issue is an instrument, not a description — give the corpus the rule
input.body:
An issue *I* will act on is a description. An issue a **person** will act on is an instrument: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is not the next click is in the way. The corpus does not distinguish them, so they get written the same way — and the reader skims, loses the thread, and does three of six steps.

The prompting artifact was [missingbulb/Shepherd#352](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/352): six checkboxes with an explanatory paragraph under each, plus a breadcrumb trail (`Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables`) where a link belonged, and two steps that mint a value shown exactly once without saying so.

## What is already there, and what is missing

`basics` requires such work to get **its own issue**, with a checkbox per step, what breaks while each is off, and a closing condition. That is *what the issue contains*. Nothing says how it is laid out — and the `breaks` requirement, read literally, is what puts a paragraph under every checkbox.

Three skills each re-spell a fragment of the shape and none owns it: `verify-in-production` ("a checkbox per step — the exact URL to open…"), `writing-migration-plans`, and lifecycle's `adopt-pack` (which says to carry each step's `breaks` and `done` into the checklist, i.e. the defect, as instruction).

## Scope

- [ ] One skill in `basics` owning how a human-executed issue is written; the three above point at it rather than re-spelling.
- [ ] The body is a checklist and nothing else — every explanation below the last box, `breaks` and `done` included.
- [ ] One imperative line per box, and a bar for when a box is carrying an explanation.
- [ ] The deepest URL that lands on the screen, never a settings breadcrumb, with the real owner and repo substituted.
- [ ] A step producing a value names the control that mints it, where on that screen it appears, and whether it is shown once.
- [ ] Ordering: walk the list as the reader and check each step is doable when reached.
- [ ] Drop boxes that are usually no-ops — they teach the reader to skim the list that exists to stop them skimming.

No check: these are GitHub issue bodies, not repo files, so nothing deterministic can see them. Skill is the strongest available rung.

## Done when

`#352` reads as a checklist a person can work top to bottom, and the next handover written from the corpus comes out the same way.

input.head: claude/writing-handover-issues-skill
input.body:
Closes #1531

An issue you will act on is a description. An issue a **person** will act on is an instrument — they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is not the next click is in the way. The corpus does not distinguish them, so they come out the same, and the reader skims and does three of six steps.

## The rule

The body has exactly two parts: a checklist of imperative one-line boxes, and — below the last box — everything else. What each step buys, what stays broken while it is undone, why the task exists: all of it after the checklist, none of it between the boxes.

Each box carries **the deepest URL that lands on the screen**, with the real owner and repo substituted, rather than a `Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables` breadcrumb. A box that *produces* a value names the control that mints it, where on that screen the value then appears, and whether it is shown only once — the step that goes wrong, because the writer knows the page and the reader does not.

Plus: order so each step is doable when reached; drop boxes that are usually no-ops, since they teach the reader to skim the list that exists to stop them skimming; close with one observable.

## What moved, not what was added

`basics` already required a handover to carry each step's `breaks` and its closing condition. That requirement stands — read literally, it is also what puts a paragraph under every checkbox, so the skill sends it below the checklist instead. Nothing a handover must state is dropped.

`verify-in-production`, `writing-migration-plans` and lifecycle's `adopt-pack` each re-spelled a fragment of the shape and none owned it; all three now point here. `adopt-pack`'s change is substantive — it told you to carry `breaks` and `done` into the checklist, which is the defect as instruction.

## No check

These are GitHub issue bodies, not repo files, so nothing deterministic can see them. Skill is the strongest rung available.

input.body:
Closes #942

Turning the dashboard's sign-in on needed a serverless function pasted in by hand and three values set beside it — the step that reliably does not happen, which is why every deployment still falls back to the token box.

`claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange` makes it a run.

## The task

Uploads `oauth-exchange.mjs` to Cloudflare Workers with its three bindings, enables the `workers.dev` route (previews off — a preview URL is a second origin able to mint tokens), and then **probes the URL** before reporting success: a stranger's origin must be refused `403 origin_not_allowed`, the allowed origin with no code must get `400 missing_code`. Only those two answers together show the route is live, the handler is this one, and the allowlist is the one just uploaded — none of which the upload's own 200 says. A fresh route takes seconds to propagate, so a miss is retried before it is believed.

`frequency: 'manual'`, `agent_model: 'none'`. The endpoint changes when its source, its client secret or its allowed origins change; none of those is a cadence, so nothing instantiates it and the only way it runs is a work item somebody creates.

It does not set the exchange URL. The endpoint is live the moment it deploys, but the button appears only once the deployment names the URL — so the run prints the exact value.

## Where each value lives, by what it actually is

| Store | Name | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| Actions secret | `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` | a real credential; **Account · Workers Scripts · Edit**, nothing else |
| Actions secret | `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | a real credential |
| Repo variable | `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` | in every Cloudflare dashboard URL its owner opens |
| Repo variable | `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID` | in every authorize URL the page builds |
| Repo variable | `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL` | fetched by the browser; and minted by a deploy rather than authored |
| Declaration | `allowedOrigins`, `workerName` | optional, deploy-only, and reviewable in a diff |

The three variables are possible because of #1494, which hands every repository variable to code-work. The two sign-in ones also needed the seeded Pages workflow to pass them, since that workflow — not the executor — is the site build's host.

**The cache key was the trap.** That workflow skips the build when a hash over the mount and settings is unchanged, and no file hash covers a repository variable. Without folding them into the key, changing either would hit the cache, skip the build, and leave the site serving the previous client id with nothing to show for it. They are hashed in, so a value's own characters cannot break the key.

One reader, `deployment-config.mjs`, resolves the pair for both the site build and the deploy task, so the endpoint cannot be minted for a different App than the button authorizes against. A declaration still carrying `clientId`/`exchangeUrl` is read as the fallback and reported once — nothing converges a member's settings file, so a deployment configured before this keeps its button.

## For an existing member

The seeded `claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml` needs re-seeding from the new stub before a variable reaches its build. `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so that is a PR someone merges, once, per repo already running the dashboard. [missingbulb/Shepherd#352](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/352) carries it as a step.

## Also here

`oauth-exchange.example.mjs` → `oauth-exchange.mjs`: it is the file a deploy uploads now, not an illustration of one. The endpoint's own source is otherwise unchanged.

The `writing-handover-issues` skill this work prompted is [#1532](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1532), split out — the two share no file.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
